ai.summary: VS Code is a very large Electron application organised by layer rather than by feature. src/vs splits into base, platform, editor, workbench and sessions, each allowed to depend only on the layers below it. extensions holds the built-in extensions, which use the same public API third parties do, and build, cli and test carry the packaging pipeline, the Rust CLI and the automation suites.

strengths: The layer rule is the architecture: base, platform, editor, workbench and sessions may only depend downwards, which is what keeps a codebase this size navigable.
Built-in features are extensions using the public API, so the extension surface is exercised by the product itself.
The same source produces a desktop app, a server for remote development, a browser build and the standalone Monaco editor.
Testing runs at several levels: unit tests inside src, API tests as an extension, and smoke tests that drive a real build through the automation driver.
The proposed API mechanism gives new extension surface a staging area instead of shipping it as stable immediately.
concerns: Nineteen thousand files with src/vs/workbench alone holding nearly five thousand; no newcomer can hold the tree in their head, and the layer documentation is the only usable map.
Over 21,000 open issues and pull requests are attached to the repository, so the tracker is a corpus rather than a work queue.
extensions/copilot is more than half of the extensions directory, which unbalances what looks like a directory of peers.
The repository mixes TypeScript, Rust and several bundlers (gulp, vite, rspack appear side by side under build), so the build story is layered rather than single.
Source and tests are split between in-tree unit tests and the separate test directory, so the suite for a given change is not always obvious.
